mechanism: Four well-documented pricing biases: loss framing (state what the buyer loses by waiting), per-day reframing (split a total into a small daily figure), a free gift in place of a discount (protects the anchor price), and a trimmed menu (fewer options reduces choice overload). They are applied as copy edits to a price line or offer, not as software. The effect comes from how buyers weigh losses and small recurring amounts against a lump sum.
claim: A carousel claims these framings change what people pay and accept.
why_not_testable: Measuring any effect needs real recipients or an audience, and there is no keyless public dataset to check it against tonight.
needs: A real audience or send list to A/B the copy on.
one_line: Four old pricing-psychology tricks (loss framing, per-day price, gift over discount, fewer options) packaged as a copy kit for offers and proposals.
idea_why: These biases are replicated in the behavioural economics literature, though effect sizes vary by context.
breakdown: Write a one-page kit with a before and after line for each of the four framings, using real offer text. Make two versions of the same proposal or email, one plain and one framed, and send each to a comparable half of a list. Count replies or accepts per version; a hired person would only be needed to supply the list and read the replies. Claude Code can draft the variants and keep the log.

mechanism: Harp is a Warp fork whose sidebar shows per-tab agent state (working, waiting, done). Rate-limit rings for Claude Code come from the status line: Claude Code passes plan limit data only to its configured statusLine command, so Harp installs one in ~/.claude/settings.json that saves that input to a file the app reads. Codex limits are parsed from rate_limits entries in its session logs under ~/.codex/sessions. Groups are stored as tmux session options so they survive restarts.

one_line: A Warp fork that reads Claude Code's status line input to draw 5 hour and weekly limit rings next to each agent session.
idea_why: Using the status line as the only supported channel for plan limit data is a plain, low-risk way to get that number.
breakdown: The reusable piece is small: a status line command that writes its stdin JSON to a file, and a reader that turns the limit fields into a percentage. A launchd job or menu bar script could poll that file and notify when a window is nearly spent. Agent state could come from hook events (Notification, Stop) written to a log. No server or account is needed.

mechanism: In LLM-assisted digital forensics the evidence is attacker-controlled and must be read, so text planted on a seized device reaches the model as instructions. The paper's taxonomy has four parts: objective, technique, payload location and concealment. The enabling fact is a perception gap, where deterministic tools, the human examiner and the model each see the same bytes differently. Three demonstrated attacks change a reported conclusion, write attacker-chosen content to the analyst's workstation, and cause outbound network traffic.
claim: Text planted on evidence can steer an LLM forensic pipeline, shown with three working attacks and proposed mitigations.
why_not_testable: Reproducing it needs model answers, and there is no local LLM on this Mac.
needs: A model endpoint and the authors' pipeline.
one_line: Forensic evidence is attacker-written by definition, so any LLM that reads it can be steered by text planted on the seized device.
idea_why: It is the standard indirect injection problem applied to a setting where reading the hostile content is mandatory.
breakdown: To check it, build a small fake evidence set with planted instruction strings in file names, document text and metadata. Run it through an agent with a tool-using summariser and note which locations change the output. The mitigations are separating reading from acting, stripping or escaping evidence text, and requiring a deterministic check on any conclusion. Proteus's own agents read stranger-written bodies every night, so the same hygiene applies here.

mechanism: Keep a short named list of senders or event types that may interrupt now, and route everything else into two scheduled digests, a morning brief and an evening rundown. The mechanism is a filter plus a batcher: classify each incoming event, push only if it is on the list, otherwise append to a queue that is flushed twice a day. Counting pushes per day first gives the baseline to judge the change against.
claim: Interruptions cost focus, so only a VIP list should notify and the rest should wait for a digest.

idea_why: Allow-list interruption with batched digests is a simple, well-understood design that cuts noise.
breakdown: Count the pushes an agent sends in a week and tag each as urgent or not. Write the VIP rules (a few sender or event types) in a config file. mechanism: Omnara runs the agent loop on a server and stores each agent's state in Postgres, so an agent survives restarts and costs nothing while idle. Clients message an agent and stream its events over an API. Sandboxes run commands, and secrets, permissions and role-based access are handled by the server. The harness has the usual file and shell tools, subagents, compaction, MCP, skills and memory, and can use a laptop as one of its machines.
claim: An open-source, self-hostable equivalent of Claude Managed Agents with durable, event-sourced agents; 107 points on Show HN.
why_not_testable: It needs Postgres, a sandbox runtime and a model key, and there is no local LLM here.
needs: A model API key, Postgres and a sandbox runtime.
one_line: An open durable-agent server that keeps every agent's state in Postgres, so it survives restarts and costs nothing idle.
idea_why: Persisting the event log of an agent is a proven way to get resumability and cheap idle time.
breakdown: The pattern is an append-only event log per agent, a loop that replays it to rebuild context, and tool calls executed in a sandbox. Proteus already approximates it with state files and a runlock. To try it, self-host the repo with Postgres and a hosted model key, create one agent by API call and kill and restart the server to see whether it resumes. A person would handle hosting and secrets.

mechanism: DynaWeave takes static agent tasks and adds exogenous events (changed requirements, environment state or outside information) as a directed acyclic graph of events with dependencies. An execution engine fires them during the agent's run. A dynamic verifier revises only the checks that the fired events affect and keeps the rest. 2,095 verified trajectories over 36 environments were used for supervised fine-tuning of Qwen3.5 models.
claim: Fine-tuning on dynamic scenarios raised CostBench task completion by 67.34 percentage points and beat Gemini-3.1-Pro-Preview on ToolMaze.
why_not_testable: It needs model fine-tuning and benchmark runs; there is no local LLM.
one_line: Agent training tasks get random mid-run twists, and only the checks those twists affect are re-scored; one benchmark jumped 67 points.
idea_why: The method is plausible but the headline gain is from the authors' own benchmark choices.
breakdown: The test-harness idea transfers without training: take an existing task with a checker, add one scripted mid-run change, and rerun the check only for what the change touches. That could be used to test Proteus's own nightly agents against surprises like a source going down. The paper's code is public for the full version.
